summary: Explains how Mobile IPv4 can work together with IPsec-based VPN gateways for enterprise users who roam while connected remotely. It gives an applicability statement for combining the two and defines a secure way for a device to detect whether it is on the trusted internal network. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Picture an employee who walks between buildings while holding a secure tunnel back to the office. This explains how to keep that private tunnel working as the person moves, and how the device can tell when it is already inside.

why does ipsec need renegotiation when a device moves
subtitle: How a roaming laptop keeps its sessions alive across networks while still using an IPsec VPN, and how it safely knows when it is back inside.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv4 and IPsec do not work together well: an IPsec tunnel must be renegotiated whenever the device changes address, yet enterprise users want to roam between internal and external networks without dropping sessions.
tldr.mechanism: Run a second Mobile IPv4 layer under the IPsec tunnel while outside, use plain Mobile IPv4 with the internal home agent while inside, and let the device prove it is inside by a registration whose reply carries a new Trusted Networks Configured extension.
tldr.outcome: IPsec never sees the device move, with no change to VPN gateways or foreign agents, but an external home agent is needed and packet overhead and complexity go up.

today: RFC 5265 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself notes that MOBIKE (RFC 4555) would remove the need for the external Mobile IPv4 layer, but that it requires VPN device changes.

sections.title: The Goal and the Two-Part Solution
sections.content:
RFC 5265 tackles the Mobile IPv4 (MIPv4) and IPsec coexistence problem for enterprise users, which was first described in RFC 4093. The goal is seamless session mobility between subnets, whether they belong to the internal (trusted) network or the external (untrusted) one.

The document has two parts. The first is an applicability statement for combining MIPv4 and IPsec for corporate remote access. The second is a technical specification and set of requirements for securely detecting whether the mobile node is on the internal or the external network, including one new extension that the mobile node and the internal home agent must implement.

The solution assumes it must minimize changes to existing firewall, VPN and DMZ deployments, must not route traffic through the DMZ when the mobile node is inside, and must support foreign networks that offer only foreign agent access. It covers IPv4 only, and an IPsec-based remote access VPN only.
sections.plainLanguage: People want to move around between the office and outside without their connection breaking. This paper shows how to do that with the locks the company already has, plus one new trick to know where you are.

sections.title: Why IPsec Lacks Mobility
sections.content:
An IPsec security association is one-way and is identified by three things: the destination address, the security protocol (ESP or AH) and the Security Parameter Index (SPI). When a mobile peer sends to a stationary peer, nothing breaks, because the stationary peer owns the association. The trouble comes in the other direction: the destination address was fixed during IKE negotiation as the mobile peer's care-of address at that moment, so packets keep going to the old address after the device moves.

IPsec NAT traversal can give limited mobility, but UDP tunneling would be needed even without a NAT, and support for changed NAT mappings is not required. The RFC therefore assumes that any change in the addresses that make up an association needs a new IKE negotiation, which costs too much computation and latency for useful mobility.

The RFC notes that the IKEv2 Mobility and Multihoming Protocol (MOBIKE, RFC 4555) would let the external Mobile IPv4 layer be removed, but it needs changes to VPN devices and so is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The secure tunnel remembers your exact street address. When you move house, the mail still goes to the old one until you set up the tunnel all over again, which takes too long.

sections.title: The Network Environment and Access Modes
sections.content:
A typical corporate network has three domains: the Internet (untrusted external network), the intranet (trusted internal network) and the DMZ between them. Access to the inside is guarded by a firewall and a VPN device. The document uses short names for the pieces: i-HA and x-HA are the internal and external home agents, and VPN-TIA is the VPN tunnel inner address.

Each way the mobile node can attach is called an access mode, written as three positions: the external MIP layer (f for foreign agent care-of address, c for co-located care-of address), a v if the VPN is used, and the internal MIP mode. That gives four modes: c and f (inside, plain Mobile IPv4) and cvc and fvc (outside, through the VPN).

Outside, the mobile node registers its care-of address with the x-HA, builds an IPsec tunnel with IKE if it has no security association yet, and then registers the VPN-TIA as a co-located care-of address with the i-HA from inside the tunnel. Reverse tunneling (the T-bit) SHOULD be set for the inner registration, because IPsec selectors usually only allow the VPN-TIA as the client address and packets from the home address would otherwise be dropped. The mobile node MUST NOT skip the VPN layer, even if it uses triangular routing.

NAT traversal SHOULD be supported for the external and internal MIP layers and for the VPN layer, since NAT devices can affect each layer independently.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside the office you just walk around. Outside, you first tell a helper where you are, then open a locked tunnel to the office, then tell the office helper where the tunnel ends. If your location changes, only the first helper needs to hear about it.

sections.title: Detecting the Internal Network
sections.content:
Secure detection matters because a mobile node that wrongly thinks it is inside would send plaintext over an untrusted network. Overall security is therefore the lesser of IPsec's security and the security of the detection mechanism. Leaving the internal network is the harder event to notice, for example after an upstream routing change or an undetected 802.11 reassociation.

The requirements are strict. The mobile node MUST track each interface separately, MUST stop relaying user data when an interface's status changes and resume only after detection and registrations are done, and MUST NOT conclude that it is inside unless a registration with the i-HA succeeded, the reply held a Trusted Networks Configured extension and the interface status has not changed since. While inside it MUST NOT send or receive user data if more than T_MONITOR seconds have passed since the last successful re-registration. T_MONITOR MUST be configurable and defaults to 60 seconds.

The proposed algorithm sends two registration requests at once, one to the i-HA and one to the x-HA, and retransmits both until answered. A reply from the x-HA means the node tentatively decides it is outside, though it keeps retrying the i-HA for a while and MAY delay IPsec setup. A reply from the i-HA carrying the extension means it SHOULD decide it is inside, and it then stops retransmitting to both. The i-HA and x-HA addresses MUST be different.

The design relies on the enterprise firewall blocking traffic from external networks to the i-HA, so that a plaintext registration can only succeed from inside. The i-HA adds a second safeguard using the extension described next.
sections.plainLanguage: Before taking off your coat in the office, you check that you really are in the office by getting a password-protected answer from the front desk. You also check again every minute, in case someone moved you.

sections.title: The Trusted Networks Configured Extension
sections.content:
The Trusted Networks Configured (TNC) extension is a skippable extension in the short format of Mobile IPv4 (RFC 3344). The i-HA includes it in a registration reply to tell the mobile node that it checks source addresses against a configured list of trusted networks.

It is four bytes: Type 149, Length 2, Sub-Type 0, and a Reserved byte that is set to 0 when sending and ignored on receipt. IANA has assigned the Type and Sub-Type, and new Sub-Types are allocated by Expert Review and Specification Required.

The extension exists so that a firewall mistake alone cannot silently expose user data. Both the firewall and the i-HA would have to be misconfigured for that to happen.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a tiny stamp that the office helper adds to its answer, meaning: I only talk to people I know are inside the building.

sections.title: Requirements for Each Component
sections.content:
The mobile node MUST implement an internal network detection algorithm meeting the requirements above, MUST support access modes c, f, cvc and fvc, and MUST NOT disable IPsec protection unless the i-HA reply contains the TNC extension. When outside, IPsec policy MUST encrypt all traffic to and from the enterprise network. When it can reach the i-HA directly, it SHOULD use only the inner Mobile IPv4 layer.

The VPN device security policy MUST allow UDP to the internal home agents on port 434 with any remote port, and SHOULD also allow IP-IP to them.

The internal home agent MUST be configured with a list of trusted IP subnets, with none trusted by default. It MUST silently drop any registration request from outside those subnets (and SHOULD log them), and it MUST add the TNC extension to replies to requests from trusted addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone gets a short rule list. The traveller must check where it is, the tunnel door must let registration messages through, and the office helper must only answer people from trusted rooms.

sections.title: Packet Overhead and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The maximum packet overhead depends on access mode: 0 octets for f, 20 for c, 77 for fvc and 97 for cvc. In cvc the 97 octets are 20 for the inner IP-IP, 57 for IPsec ESP and 20 for the outer IP-IP. The ESP figure assumes a 64-bit block cipher and a 12-octet authentication field. NAT traversal adds more, bringing the worst case for cvc to 129 octets.

Latency inside is no worse than standard MIPv4 if the parallel registration is used. Outside, initial setup adds the x-HA registration, optional detection delay and IKE setup, but handovers in the external network are comparable to standard MIPv4, because the node just re-registers with the x-HA and keeps sending IPsec traffic to the VPN gateway from its new address.

The costs are an external home agent, two parallel MIPv4 layers, three tunneling layers in the mobile node and possible firewall state problems when moving between inside and outside. The RFC also says the solution can work with non-IPsec VPNs, but does not consider them explicitly.
sections.plainLanguage: Wrapping a parcel in extra boxes keeps it safe but makes it heavier. The most boxes you add here is 97 units of wrapping, and a little more if the mail has to get past a middle-man.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If the mobile node wrongly believes it is inside, it compromises IPsec. Detection relies on a successful i-HA registration, which for standard MIPv4 means HMAC-MD5 and replay protection, plus the firewall blocking outside access to the i-HA. The i-HA's trusted-source list and the TNC extension mean that both the firewall and the i-HA must be misconfigured before data is exposed. A weak MIPv4 shared secret on the i-HA is described as fatal, since the node could be fooled into dropping encryption.

A registration sent in plaintext from an untrusted network reveals the i-HA address, the node's identity including its NAI and home address, and the authenticator value.

The external MIPv4 layer can open traffic redirection attacks against IPsec traffic, including the transient pseudo-NAT attack, although these cannot compromise the confidentiality of IPsec-protected data. Combining MIPv4 and IPsec also mixes algorithms and key management models, and adds complexity.
sections.plainLanguage: The risk is being tricked into thinking you are safely inside and taking off your armour outside. The rules make that need two separate mistakes at once, and the paper lists what an attacker could still learn or redirect.
